passage:
Tuesday
Today Sudha tore my drawing and called me a copycat in front of everyone. My hands went hot and I wanted to push her so badly. 😠 I remembered what Ammi says: count to ten, then decide. I counted. By seven my hands were still shaking but I didn't push. I said, "That was my drawing. That hurt." Sudha looked surprised and walked away. Later she said sorry. I'm still angry, a bit. But I'm glad I didn't hit her. I would be the one in trouble.
— Nazia

qa.q: What did Sudha call Nazia?
qa.a: Sudha called Nazia a copycat.

qa.q: What does Nazia's hot, shaking hands show about Nazia's feelings?
qa.a: They show Nazia was very angry and wanted to push Sudha.

qa.q: Which choice by Nazia worked, and why?
qa.a: Nazia counted before acting and then used words, which stopped a fight and led Sudha to apologise.

qa.q: How might Sudha have felt when Nazia said "That hurt"?
qa.a: She may have been surprised and realised she had really upset Nazia.

grounding: A diary shows a child pausing before retaliating and choosing words instead of pushing.

passage: The evening queue at the hand-pump near the village temple was long, and everyone was tired. Tanuja had waited twenty minutes with her brass pot. When she finally reached the front, Shalini splashed muddy water on Tanuja's clean frock and laughed. "Oops, now you match the buffaloes!" Some girls giggled. Tanuja's fists clenched. She stepped forward. Then she stopped, took a slow breath and looked at her frock. "That wasn't funny. My mother washed this today." Shalini's grin faded. Tanuja filled her pot and walked away with her chin up.

qa.q: Where did Shalini splash muddy water on Tanuja?
qa.a: At the hand-pump near the village temple.

qa.q: What does Tanuja stepping forward and then stopping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was very angry and tempted to hit back but chose to hold herself back.

qa.q: What did Tanuja do instead of retaliating?
qa.a: She took a slow breath and told Shalini clearly that it wasn't funny.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when that grin fades?
qa.a: Shalini might realise the joke hurt and feel a little embarrassed.

grounding: It shows a child delaying her response to provocation and choosing words over blows.

passage: In the Sunday league match in Leeds, Yuki tripped Felix from behind and whispered, "Too slow." Felix hit the grass hard. He jumped up, fists tight, and took a step towards Yuki. His heart was pounding. Then he stopped, looked at the referee and breathed out slowly. "Ref, that was a foul," he said. The referee blew her whistle and gave Felix a free kick. Yuki shrugged. Felix placed the ball carefully and scored.

qa.q: What did Yuki whisper after tripping Felix?
qa.a: Yuki whispered, "Too slow."

qa.q: What does Felix's pounding heart and tight fists show?
qa.a: They show he was angry and ready to fight back.

qa.q: What helped Felix avoid a fight?
qa.a: He paused, breathed out slowly and told the referee instead of hitting Yuki.

qa.q: How might Felix's teammates see his choice?
qa.a: They may respect him for staying calm and winning the free kick instead of getting sent off.

grounding: It shows a child pausing before retaliating and choosing words over a fight.

passage: The whistle had just gone at the sports club when Hrithik trotted past and flicked Tejas's water bottle into the mud. 'Oops, butterfingers,' he grinned. Tejas, eleven, felt heat race up his neck. His hand balled into a fist. He took one step, then stopped. He looked at the coach's shed, then down at his boots, and let out a long breath. He picked up the bottle, wiped it on his shorts and walked back. 'Hrithik, don't touch my stuff again. It's not funny.' Hrithik shrugged and jogged off. Later, Coach Mathew squeezed Tejas's shoulder. 'I saw that. Took more strength than kicking a ball.' Tejas nodded, jaw still tight.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do to Tejas's water bottle?
qa.a: He flicked it into the mud and said, 'Oops, butterfingers.'

qa.q: What does Tejas's tight jaw at the end suggest?
qa.a: He was still angry inside even after choosing words, so holding back cost him real effort.

qa.q: What helped Tejas pause before hitting back?
qa.a: Stopping after one step, looking away and letting out a long breath gave him time to choose words instead of blows.

qa.q: How might Coach Mathew see Tejas's choice?
qa.a: He sees it as a sign of real strength and self-control, not weakness, which is why he praised him.

grounding: Shows a child delaying a response to provocation and choosing words over blows.

passage: I'm Minakshi, and I sit behind Sharmila in class five. In the lunch queue yesterday, a boy from the other section shoved her from behind and called her 'slowpoke'. Her tiffin nearly fell. I saw her turn around fast and her hand went up. I thought she was going to push him back, honestly. But she just held her hand there for a second, pressed her lips together and put it down. Then she said, loud and clear, 'Don't push me. Wait your turn.' The boy looked surprised and stepped back. I don't know what she was thinking in that second. Afterwards she ate her lunch very quietly. I shared my mango pickle with her.

qa.q: What did the boy call Sharmila in the lunch queue?
qa.a: He called her 'slowpoke'.

qa.q: What might Sharmila have been feeling when her hand went up?
qa.a: She was probably angry and ready to push back, though Minakshi can't be sure what went on in her head.

qa.q: What worked in the way Sharmila handled the shove?
qa.a: She stopped her hand, took a moment and then used clear, firm words, which made the boy step back without a fight.

qa.q: Why might Minakshi have shared her pickle with Sharmila?
qa.a: She may have sensed Sharmila was still upset and quiet, and wanted to show kindness and support.

grounding: An observer describes a child pausing before retaliating and using words instead of a push.

passage:
Monday: At lunch, Rehana knocked Chandrika's tiffin off the bench. The rice spilled everywhere. Chandrika, ten, shoved her so hard that Rehana fell. Both were sent to the counsellor.
Wednesday: The counsellor, Mrs Pinto, taught Chandrika a trick. “When the anger comes, press your feet into the floor, count to five, then decide.”
Next Tuesday: Rehana called Chandrika “bhains” in the line. Chandrika felt the heat rush up. She pressed her feet down. One, two, three, four, five.
“That's not okay,” she said clearly, and walked to the other end of the line.

qa.q: What trick did the counsellor teach Chandrika?
qa.a: Press your feet into the floor, count to five, then decide.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel when Rehana called her a name?
qa.a: She felt anger rush up like heat, but she stayed in control.

qa.q: Why did counting to five help?
qa.a: It gave her a pause so she could choose words instead of shoving.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel when Chandrika walks away?
qa.a: She may feel surprised, since Chandrika didn't react as before.

grounding: Over a week a ten-year-old learns to pause before retaliating and use words instead.

passage:
Hrithik, you want to hit that boy back? Sit down. Let your Samir Mama tell you something.
When I was twelve, in a cricket match behind our building in Indore, a boy called Pappu said I was out when I wasn't. He laughed in my face. I threw the bat down and punched him. His nose bled. I was banned from the team for the rest of the summer.
The next year, another boy cheated. My fist closed. But I remembered that summer sitting alone on the steps. So I walked away, counted my breaths, came back and said, “Let's ask the umpire.” The umpire agreed with me.
Hitting feels quick. Pausing feels slow. But pausing worked, Hrithik. Hitting didn't.

qa.q: Where was the cricket match?
qa.a: Behind their building in Indore.

qa.q: How did young Samir feel when Pappu laughed in his face?
qa.a: He felt furious and humiliated, enough to throw down the bat and punch Pappu.

qa.q: What choice in the story worked better, and why?
qa.a: Walking away, counting breaths and asking the umpire the next year, because it solved the problem without getting him banned.

qa.q: How might Pappu have felt after being punched?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and shocked, and may have been angry or scared of Samir.

grounding: An uncle tells his nephew how he learned to pause and use words instead of fists.

passage:
The school bus was packed and noisy, and Keerthana, eleven, was squashed by the door. Pranav reached over, snatched her new cap, and held it out of the window.
“Want it? Come get it!”
Keerthana's hand flew up to slap him. The bus lurched. Everyone was watching.
She stopped. Took one breath. Lowered her hand.
“Give it back now,” she said, loud enough for the driver to hear.
The driver looked in the mirror. “Pranav!”
Pranav pulled the cap in and dropped it on her lap. “It was a joke.”
“Not a funny one,” said Keerthana, and put it on.

qa.q: What did Pranav snatch?
qa.a: Her new cap.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel when Pranav held the cap out of the window?
qa.a: She felt angry and embarrassed, her hand flying up to slap him.

qa.q: What helped Keerthana get the cap back without hitting?
qa.a: She took a breath, lowered her hand and used loud, clear words that got the driver's attention.

qa.q: How might the driver see the situation?
qa.a: The driver sees Pranav's behaviour is unsafe and unkind and steps in quickly.

grounding: On a crowded bus an eleven-year-old pauses and chooses words instead of a slap.

passage:
In the school bus queue in Chennai, Yamini shoved Nilesh from behind and laughed. His water bottle fell and rolled into the gutter.
Nilesh swung round, fists tight. Yamini grinned, waiting.
He stopped. He counted in his head: one, two, three, four, five. His breathing slowed a little.
"That wasn't funny," he said, voice shaking. "Pick up my bottle, or I'm telling the conductor."
Yamini's grin slipped. She rolled her eyes but fished the bottle out.
Nilesh took it and got on the bus. His hands were still trembling, but he hadn't hit anyone.

qa.q: Where did Nilesh's water bottle roll?
qa.a: Into the gutter.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when he swung round with fists tight?
qa.a: Nilesh felt angry and humiliated after being shoved and laughed at.

qa.q: What did pausing to count to five give Nilesh the chance to do?
qa.a: It gave him time to calm down enough to use firm words instead of his fists.

qa.q: How might Yamini see Nilesh's response?
qa.a: Yamini expected a fight and seemed surprised when he stayed calm and firm, which took the fun out of her joke.

grounding: A child pauses and counts before responding to a shove, choosing words over hitting.

passage:
"Your drawing looks like a baby did it," Rashmi said, loud enough for the whole playground to hear.
Nazia's hand tightened on the paper. "Take that back."
"Why? It's true."
Nazia took a step forward. Then she stopped. She turned and walked to the water tap and splashed her face.
When she came back, Rashmi was still there. "Running away?"
"No," said Nazia. "I'm choosing not to fight. What you said was mean. It hurt."
Rashmi opened her mouth, then shut it. "Fine. Whatever."
Nazia smoothed the drawing and went to show her teacher.

qa.q: Where did Nazia go after she stopped?
qa.a: To the water tap.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when her hand tightened on the paper?
qa.a: Nazia felt angry and hurt by Rashmi's mean comment.

qa.q: Which choice by Nazia worked, and why?
qa.a: Walking away to splash her face gave her time to cool down, so she could tell Rashmi calmly that it hurt instead of fighting.

qa.q: Why might Rashmi react differently than expected?
qa.a: Rashmi was ready for a fight, so Nazia calmly naming the hurt left her with nothing to say.

grounding: On a playground a child walks away to cool down, then answers an insult with words.

passage:
I still remember the day Baljeet knocked my tiffin off the table in Class 5. My rajma went everywhere. He laughed and said, "Oops."
I wanted to throw my bottle at him. My arm was already up.
But I put it down. I walked to the sink and washed my hands slowly, counting the tiles. Twelve.
When I came back, I said, "Baljeet, that was my lunch. Say sorry and help clean it."
He looked surprised. He said sorry, and even gave me half his parathas.
If I'd thrown the bottle, I'd be the one in trouble. I'm Madhuri, and I'm still a little proud of that day.

qa.q: What did Madhuri count at the sink?
qa.a: The tiles, twelve of them.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when her arm was already up?
qa.a: Madhuri felt furious and wanted to hurt Baljeet back.

qa.q: What did Madhuri's pause at the sink allow her to do?
qa.a: It gave her time to calm down so she could ask for an apology and help instead of throwing her bottle.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt when Madhuri came back calm?
qa.a: Baljeet was surprised, and Madhuri's calm, firm words likely made him feel sorry enough to share his parathas.

grounding: A young person recalls pausing before hitting back and using words instead.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5
During games, Uma snatched the ball from Ganga and called her "slowpoke". Ganga's fists clenched. Last term she would have hit.
Today she stopped, took a breath, and walked to me. "Uma called me a name and took the ball. I want to hit her but I didn't."
I thanked Ganga and spoke to Uma, who apologised and returned the ball.
I praised Ganga at circle time and let her lead the next game.

qa.q: What name did Uma call Ganga?
qa.a: "Slowpoke."

qa.q: How was Ganga feeling when her fists clenched?
qa.a: She felt angry and tempted to hit.

qa.q: What did Ganga do instead of hitting?
qa.a: She paused, took a breath, and told the teacher in words.

qa.q: How might Uma feel after apologising?
qa.a: Uma may feel embarrassed and a bit sorry.

grounding: A teacher's note records a child pausing and using words instead of hitting.

passage:
Holi, evening
Today Chandrika threw colour in my eyes on purpose after I said no. It stung and I was so angry. I wanted to push her into the mud.
I didn't. I remembered what Papa says: count to ten and walk away. I went to the tap and washed my eyes. I counted twice.
Then I went back and said, "I said no. That hurt." Chandrika said sorry, sort of.
I'm still a bit angry. But I'm glad I didn't push her. Papa hugged me when I told him.
Amandeep

qa.q: Where did Amandeep go after the colour hit?
qa.a: To the tap, to wash the eyes.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel after the colour hit?
qa.a: Amandeep felt stung and very angry, wanting to push Chandrika into the mud.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do that worked?
qa.a: Counting to ten, walking away and then using words to say it hurt.

qa.q: How might Chandrika feel after Amandeep spoke?
qa.a: Chandrika may feel a bit guilty, saying sorry.

grounding: A child's diary about pausing before retaliating and choosing words.

passage:
During the harvest festival in their village, Trisha, ten, was pushed off the swing by an older girl, Lalremsiami.
Trisha jumped up, face red, ready to shove her back. Then she saw the little kids watching.
She stopped. She took three breaths. She said loudly, "Don't push. It's my turn. You can go after me."
Lalremsiami blinked. "Fine."
Trisha swung high. The little kids clapped. Her heart was still pounding, but she felt strong.

qa.q: How many breaths did Trisha take?
qa.a: Three breaths.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel when she was pushed off?
qa.a: She felt angry, face red, ready to shove back.

qa.q: What helped Trisha choose words over blows?
qa.a: Noticing the little kids watching and taking three breaths before speaking.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel after Trisha spoke firmly?
qa.a: Lalremsiami may feel surprised and a bit embarrassed.

grounding: Shows a child delaying retaliation and choosing words when provoked.

passage:
It was the week before Halloween in Toronto, and Rafael had spent an hour carving a pumpkin for the school display. On the way in, Xin bumped it with his backpack. The pumpkin rolled off the steps and cracked.
"Oops," Xin said, grinning.
Rafael's hands balled into fists. He stepped forward. Then he stopped, took a long breath of the cold air, and counted to five like his coach had taught him.
"That took me an hour," he said, his voice shaking. "You need to say sorry."
Xin's grin faded. "It was kind of an accident. Sorry."
His cousin Ana, watching from the door, whispered, "I thought you were going to punch him."
"I wanted to," Rafael admitted.

qa.q: How long had Rafael spent carving the pumpkin?
qa.a: He had spent an hour carving it.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when his hands balled into fists?
qa.a: He felt furious and hurt, because Xin had broken the pumpkin and seemed to find it funny.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Pausing to breathe and count, then using clear words, worked because it gave Xin a chance to apologise instead of starting a fight.

qa.q: Why might Ana have expected Rafael to punch Xin?
qa.a: Ana saw his fists and how angry he looked, so she was surprised and relieved that he chose words instead.

grounding: Shows a child pausing before retaliating and choosing words when provoked.
